sections.title: Electrostatic potential — the electrical altitude

board_events.text: Electrostatic potential is electrical altitude
That climb quietly banks something we call potential to do work, and it belongs to the spot on the mountain, not to whichever stone happens to be sitting there.
A pebble and a boulder resting at the very same height both carry the same altitude number, even though the energy each holds is different, since that also depends on mass.
This bringing-in must happen slowly, so the charge never picks up speed and no kinetic energy sneaks into the bookkeeping.
V belongs to the point itself — it exists whether or not a test charge is ever placed there.
This formula quietly sets V equal to zero at infinity, so it only makes sense once that reference choice has been made.
Pick a different reference and every V value shifts by the same constant, but potential differences never change.

segments.text: <curious> Think about trekking up from Dehradun toward Mussoorie. Altitude is a strange kind of storage — the moment you let a stone go at the top, it comes crashing down all on its own, with zero effort on your part.
That climb quietly banks something we call potential to do work, and it belongs to the spot on the mountain, not to whichever stone happens to be sitting there.
A pebble and a boulder resting at the very same height both carry the same altitude number, even though the energy each one actually holds is completely different, since that depends on mass too.

Electrostatic potential borrows exactly this idea. We define V at a point as the work an external agent does per unit charge, bringing a tiny positive test charge in from infinity, all the way to that point.
That bringing-in has to happen slowly, so the charge never picks up speed and no kinetic energy sneaks into the bookkeeping — every joule of work goes purely into potential.
Burn this in: V belongs to the point itself. It is defined and exists whether or not you ever place a test charge there at all.
For a single point charge Q, this potential works out to a clean one over r dependence, scaled by the constant one over four pi epsilon zero.
Notice the reference: we quietly set V equal to zero at infinity, so this formula only makes sense once that choice has been made.
Pick a different reference point and every value of V you calculate shifts by the same constant amount — but differences in potential, which is what really drives physics, never change.

<curious> Socho ki tum Dehradun se Mussoorie ki taraf chadh rahe ho। Altitude ek ajeeb tarah ka storage hai — jaise hi tum top par pathar chhodte ho, wo apne aap neeche gir jaata hai, tumhari koi mehnat nahi lagti।
Wo chadhai chupke se kuch bank kar deti hai jise hum potential to do work kehte hain, aur ye us jagah ki property hai, na ki jo bhi pathar wahan rakha ho uski।
Ek pebble aur ek boulder, dono same height par ho, to unka altitude number bilkul same hoga, chahe har ek mein actual energy alag ho, kyunki wo unke mass par bhi depend karta hai।

Electrostatic potential bhi exactly yahi idea use karta hai। Hum kisi point par V ko define karte hain as the work an external agent does per unit charge, jab wo ek chhota positive test charge ko infinity se laata hai us point tak।
Ye laana slowly hona chahiye, taaki charge kabhi speed pick na kare aur kinetic energy is bookkeeping mein na ghus jaaye — har joule of work sirf potential mein jaata hai।
Isse dhyaan se yaad rakho: V us point ki apni property hai। Ye exist karta hai chahe tum wahan kabhi test charge rakho ya na rakho।
Ek single point charge Q ke liye, ye potential ek clean one over r dependence deta hai, jo scale hota hai constant one over four pi epsilon zero se।
Is reference ko notice karo: hum quietly V ko zero set kar dete hain infinity par, isliye ye formula tabhi kaam karta hai jab ye choice already ho chuki ho।
Koi different reference point choose karo, to V ki har value same constant amount se shift ho jaayegi — lekin potential difference, jo actually physics ko drive karta hai, wo kabhi nahi badalta।

sections.title: Potential is a scalar — add with sign, not direction

board_events.text: Potential is a scalar; fields are vectors
With several charges present, add up each one's potential with its own sign, like entries in a bank passbook.
A plus five volt contribution and a minus five volt contribution cancel to zero — no angles, no components.
Compare this to adding electric fields, which are vectors, needing both magnitude and direction for every contribution.
The second big idea: potential difference is what actually drives charge around, like water flowing from a higher tank to a lower one.
So positive charge always wants to slide from high potential toward low potential, exactly like water seeking the lower tank.

segments.text: Here's the single biggest relief in this whole subtopic: potential is a scalar. It has no direction to track at all.
When several charges sit in a region, you just add up their individual potentials, keeping each one's own plus or minus sign, the way you would total entries in a bank passbook.
A contribution of plus five volts and one of minus five volts cancel to exactly zero. No angles, no components, no vector diagrams needed.
For a whole system of charges, potential is simply this sum: one over four pi epsilon zero, times each charge divided by its own distance, added algebraically.
Compare that to adding electric fields. Fields are vectors, so you would have to track both magnitude and direction for every single contribution before combining them.
The second big idea is this: potential difference is what actually drives charge from one place to another, exactly the way water flows from a higher tank down to a lower one.
Formally, the potential difference between two points equals the work done per unit charge moving between them, written as minus the integral of the field along the path.
So positive charge always wants to slide from high potential toward low potential — the electrical equivalent of water seeking the lower tank, every single time.
Is poore subtopic ka sabse bada relief yahi hai: potential ek scalar hai। Isme koi direction track nahi karni padti।
Jab multiple charges kisi region mein ho, to tum unke individual potentials ko simply add kar dete ho, har ek ka apna plus ya minus sign rakhte hue, jaise bank passbook mein entries total karte ho।
Plus five volts ka contribution aur minus five volts ka contribution exactly zero cancel ho jaate hain। Koi angles nahi, koi components nahi, koi vector diagram ki zaroorat nahi।
Charges ke poore system ke liye, potential simply yahi sum hota hai: one over four pi epsilon zero, times har charge divided by uski apni distance, algebraically add kiya gaya।
Isko compare karo electric fields add karne se। Fields vectors hote hain, isliye tumhe har contribution ke liye magnitude aur direction dono track karni padegi, combine karne se pehle।
Doosra bada idea ye hai: potential difference hi actually charge ko ek jagah se doosri jagah drive karta hai, exactly jaise paani higher tank se lower tank ki taraf flow karta hai।
Formally, do points ke beech potential difference equal hota hai work done per unit charge unke beech move karne mein, jo likha jaata hai minus the integral of the field along the path ke roop mein।
Isliye positive charge hamesha high potential se low potential ki taraf slide hona chahta hai — electrical equivalent of paani ka lower tank dhoondna, har single baar।

board_events.text: An equipotential surface is the full set of points sitting at one shared potential value.
Walk along one of those contours and you neither climb nor descend, so the field does zero work on a charge moving along it.
The electric field is always perpendicular to the equipotential surface, pointing straight downhill toward decreasing potential.
Where contour lines crowd together near the charge, the field is strong; where they spread apart, it weakens.

segments.text: Let's turn the mountain picture into something you can actually draw.
Picture the field around a positive charge as a hill with the charge sitting right on the peak. Potential is simply the height of the ground at every point around it.
Draw the contour lines you would see on a trekking map, each joining points at exactly the same height — those contour lines are exactly what we call equipotential surfaces.
An equipotential surface is the full set of points sitting at one shared potential value, nothing more exotic than a single contour line.
Walk along one of those contours and you neither climb nor descend, so the field does exactly zero work on a charge moving along it.

And just like the steepest descent on a real hill is always perpendicular to its contour lines, the electric field is always perpendicular to the equipotential surface, pointing straight downhill toward lower potential.
Notice one more thing from the picture: where the contour lines crowd close together near the charge, the field is strong, and where they spread apart far away, the field grows weak.
Chalo mountain wali picture ko kuch aisa banate hain jo tum actually draw kar sako।
Socho ki positive charge ke around field ek hill jaisa hai, charge uske peak par baitha hai। Potential simply har point par zameen ki height hai।

Wo contour lines draw karo jo tum trekking map par dekhte ho, har ek line un points ko jodti hai jo exactly same height par hain। Wahi contour lines exactly wo hain jinhe hum equipotential surfaces kehte hain।
Ek equipotential surface bas un sab points ka poora set hai jo ek shared potential value par baithe hain, kuch aur exotic nahi, ek single contour line se zyada kuch nahi।
Un contours mein se kisi ek par chalo, to tum na chadhte ho na utarte ho, isliye field us par move karte charge par exactly zero work karta hai।

Aur jaise real hill par steepest descent hamesha uske contour lines ke perpendicular hota hai, waise hi electric field hamesha equipotential surface ke perpendicular hota hai, seedha downhill point karta hua lower potential ki taraf।
Picture se ek aur baat notice karo: jahan contour lines charge ke paas crowd karti hain, wahan field strong hota hai, aur jahan wo door spread ho jaati hain, wahan field weak ho jaata hai।

board_events.text: Formula toolkit: potential and superposition
Q carries its own sign, r is the distance from source to point, and epsilon zero is the permittivity of free space.
The S I unit of potential is the volt, equal to one joule per coulomb.
That superposition is purely algebraic — no vectors, no angles, just signed numbers added directly.

board_events.latex: W_{A\to B} = q(V_B - V_A) = q\,\Delta V

board_events.text: The reference constant, one over four pi epsilon zero, equals nine times ten to the ninth newton metre squared per coulomb squared.

segments.text: Let's collect the core formulas for this subtopic in one place.
The potential due to a single point charge is one over four pi epsilon zero, times Q over r.
Q carries its own sign straight into the answer, r is the distance from the source to the point, and epsilon zero is the permittivity of free space.
The S I unit of potential is the volt, which is exactly one joule per coulomb.
Dimensionally, potential works out to M L squared T to the minus three, A to the minus one.
For a whole system of charges, or even a continuous distribution, potential is the sum one over four pi epsilon zero, times each charge over its own distance.
That superposition is purely algebraic — no vectors, no angles, just signed numbers added straight up.
The work done moving a charge from A to B is that charge times the potential difference: q times V B minus V A, or simply q delta V.
And the reference constant, one over four pi epsilon zero, comes out to nine times ten to the power nine newton metre squared per coulomb squared.
Chalo is subtopic ke core formulas ek jagah collect karte hain।
Single point charge ki wajah se potential hota hai one over four pi epsilon zero, times Q over r.
Q apna sign seedha answer mein le jaata hai, r source se point tak ki distance hai, aur epsilon zero permittivity of free space hai।
Potential ka S I unit volt hai, jo exactly one joule per coulomb ke barabar hai।
Dimensionally, potential nikal ke aata hai M L squared T to the minus three, A to the minus one।
Charges ke poore system ke liye, ya continuous distribution ke liye bhi, potential ye sum hota hai: one over four pi epsilon zero, times har charge over apni distance।
Wo superposition purely algebraic hota hai — koi vectors nahi, koi angles nahi, sirf signed numbers seedhe add kiye jaate hain।
A se B tak charge move karne mein hua work equal hota hai us charge times potential difference ke: q times V B minus V A, ya simply q delta V.
Aur wo reference constant, one over four pi epsilon zero, nikal ke aata hai nine times ten to the power nine newton metre squared per coulomb squared.

board_events.text: Dipole potential and E equals minus dV by dr
On the axis, where theta is zero, this reaches its maximum value, p over four pi epsilon zero r squared.
On the equatorial plane, where theta is ninety degrees, the potential is exactly zero, no matter how close you stand.
Two a is the separation between the two charges, and the moment carries units of coulomb metre.
The minus sign says the field points toward decreasing potential — never forget it.
Electric field carries units of volt per metre, the same as newton per coulomb.

segments.text: Two more formulas round out this subtopic's toolkit: the dipole's potential, and the deep link between field and potential.
The potential of a short dipole at distance r, at angle theta from its axis, is one over four pi epsilon zero, times p cosine theta over r squared.
On the axis, where theta is zero, cosine theta is one, so this potential reaches its maximum value, p over four pi epsilon zero r squared.
On the equatorial plane, where theta is ninety degrees, cosine theta is zero, so the potential there is exactly zero, no matter how close you stand.
The dipole moment itself is defined as p equals q times two a.
Here, two a is the separation between the two charges, and the moment carries units of coulomb metre.
The other formula tying this whole subtopic together is E equals minus d V by d r.
That minus sign is not decoration. It tells you the field always points toward decreasing potential, downhill, every single time.
Electric field carries units of volt per metre, which works out to be exactly the same as newton per coulomb.
Do aur formulas is subtopic ke toolkit ko complete karte hain: dipole ka potential, aur field aur potential ke beech ka deep link।
Short dipole ka potential distance r par, axis se angle theta par, hota hai one over four pi epsilon zero, times p cosine theta over r squared.
Axis par, jahan theta zero hai, cosine theta one hota hai, isliye ye potential apna maximum value reach karta hai, p over four pi epsilon zero r squared.
Equatorial plane par, jahan theta ninety degrees hai, cosine theta zero hota hai, isliye wahan potential exactly zero hota hai, chahe tum kitne bhi paas khade ho।
Dipole moment khud define hota hai as p equals q times two a.
Yahan, two a do charges ke beech ki separation hai, aur moment ka unit coulomb metre hota hai।
Doosra formula jo is poore subtopic ko tie karta hai wo hai E equals minus d V by d r.
Wo minus sign koi decoration nahi hai। Ye batata hai ki field hamesha decreasing potential ki taraf point karta hai, downhill, har single baar।
Electric field ke units hote hain volt per metre, jo exactly newton per coulomb ke barabar nikalta hai।

sections.title: Deriving V equals kQ over r for a point charge

board_events.text: Derivation: potential due to a point charge
Setup: place charge plus Q at the origin, bring a test charge q-naught from infinity to point P at distance r, with V equal to zero at infinity.
This field pushes the test charge outward, so an external agent must apply an equal and opposite force to move it inward without acceleration.
The leading minus sign converts work against the field into potential, and the radial path makes the dot product simply E dx.
The whole derivation collapses to a single clean fraction, once the integral is done.
A negative source charge simply carries its sign through, giving a negative potential, consistent with potential being a signed scalar.

segments.text: Let's actually derive the formula we have been using, rather than just quoting it.
Set up the scene: place a charge plus Q at the origin, and bring a test charge q-naught from infinity to a point P at distance r, taking potential to be zero at infinity.
At some intermediate distance x from Q, the field has magnitude one over four pi epsilon zero, times Q over x squared.
This field pushes the test charge outward, so to move it inward without any acceleration, an external agent has to apply a force that is equal and opposite to that push.
By definition, potential is the work done per unit charge against the field, written as minus the integral of E d x, from infinity in to r.
That leading minus sign converts work done against the field into potential, and because the path is radial, the dot product collapses simply to E d x.
Carrying out that integral from infinity to r gives exactly the formula you already know: V equals one over four pi epsilon zero, times Q over r.
It's worth pausing on that result — the whole derivation collapses to a single clean fraction, once the integral is done.
One last check: a negative source charge simply carries its own sign straight through the formula, giving a negative potential — completely consistent with potential being a signed scalar.
Chalo actually derive karte hain wo formula jo hum ab tak use kar rahe the, na ki bas quote karte rahen।
Scene set karo: charge plus Q ko origin par rakho, aur ek test charge q-naught ko infinity se point P tak distance r par lao, potential ko infinity par zero maan kar।
Kisi intermediate distance x par Q se, field ka magnitude hota hai one over four pi epsilon zero, times Q over x squared.
Ye field test charge ko outward push karta hai, isliye use inward move karne ke liye without acceleration, external agent ko ek force apply karni padti hai jo equal and opposite ho us push ke।
By definition, potential hota hai work done per unit charge against the field, jo likha jaata hai minus the integral of E d x, infinity se r tak।
Wo leading minus sign work done against the field ko potential mein convert karta hai, aur kyunki path radial hai, dot product simply E d x mein collapse ho jaata hai।
Us integral ko infinity se r tak carry out karne se exactly wahi formula milta hai jo tum already jaante ho: V equals one over four pi epsilon zero, times Q over r.
Is result par thoda ruk kar sochna zaroori hai — poori derivation ek clean fraction mein collapse ho jaati hai, integral complete hone ke baad।
Ek last check: negative source charge apna sign seedha formula mein carry karta hai, negative potential deta hai — jo completely consistent hai potential ke signed scalar hone ke saath।

segments.text: Now let's derive the single most useful equation linking field and potential.
Picture two closely spaced equipotential surfaces, with the field running perpendicular between them, exactly as shown here.
Let surface A sit at potential V, and surface B sit at potential V plus a small delta V, separated by a tiny perpendicular distance delta l.
The field has to point straight along this perpendicular direction, because field is always normal to an equipotential surface.
Moving a unit positive charge from B across to A, against the field, costs work equal to the field's magnitude times delta l.
But that same work, moving a unit charge, is exactly the potential difference it climbs — from B up to A.
Setting those equal: the magnitude of E times delta l equals V A minus V B, which is simply minus delta V.
Taking the limit as delta l shrinks to zero turns this into E equals minus d V by d r — the field is the potential gradient, with a minus sign.
One physical payoff falls straight out: where equipotential surfaces crowd together, the field is strong, and where they spread apart, the field is weak.
Ab chalo derive karte hain sabse useful equation jo field aur potential ko link karta hai।
Socho do closely spaced equipotential surfaces, jinke beech field perpendicular chal raha hai, exactly jaisa yahan dikhaya gaya hai।
Surface A ko potential V par rakho, aur surface B ko potential V plus ek chhota delta V par, jo alag hote hain ek tiny perpendicular distance delta l se।
Field ko seedha is perpendicular direction mein point karna padega, kyunki field hamesha equipotential surface ke normal hota hai।
Ek unit positive charge ko B se A tak, field ke against move karne mein, work lagta hai equal to field ka magnitude times delta l.
Lekin wahi work, unit charge move karne mein, exactly wo potential difference hai jo wo climb karta hai — B se A tak।
Unhe equal karke: E ka magnitude times delta l equal hota hai V A minus V B ke, jo simply minus delta V hai।
Delta l ko zero tak shrink karne ki limit lete hi ye ban jaata hai E equals minus d V by d r — field potential gradient hai, ek minus sign ke saath।
Ek physical payoff seedha nikal ke aata hai: jahan equipotential surfaces paas paas crowd karti hain, wahan field strong hota hai, aur jahan wo spread ho jaati hain, field weak hota hai।

segments.text: Let's derive the dipole's potential formula from scratch.
Here is the setup: charges plus q and minus q, separated by two a, with point P sitting a distance r away, at angle theta from the axis.
We work in the far field, where r is much, much greater than a, and superpose the two point-charge potentials directly, since potential is a scalar.

That superposition gives q over four pi epsilon zero, times the quantity one over r one minus one over r two, which can be rewritten as q over four pi epsilon zero, times r two minus r one over r one r two.
Dropping a perpendicular from each charge onto the line O P is exactly how we turn those two exact distances into workable approximations.
For a short dipole, r one becomes approximately r minus a cosine theta, r two becomes r plus a cosine theta, and their product collapses to simply r squared.
That's because a is so small compared to r that the tiny correction terms barely matter once you multiply the two distances together.
Substituting these approximations, and using the dipole moment p equals two a q, the whole expression collapses to V equals one over four pi epsilon zero, times p cosine theta over r squared.
Notice this potential falls off as one over r squared, faster than a single charge's one over r, precisely because the opposite charges nearly cancel each other out at large distance.
Chalo dipole ka potential formula scratch se derive karte hain।
Yahan setup hai: charges plus q aur minus q, separated by two a, point P distance r par baitha hai, axis se angle theta par।
Hum far field mein kaam karte hain, jahan r, a se bahut zyada bada hota hai, aur dono point-charge potentials ko directly superpose karte hain, kyunki potential ek scalar hai।

Wo superposition deta hai q over four pi epsilon zero, times the quantity one over r one minus one over r two, jo rewrite ho sakta hai q over four pi epsilon zero, times r two minus r one over r one r two ke roop mein।
Har charge se line O P par perpendicular drop karna exactly wo tarika hai jisse hum un do exact distances ko workable approximations mein badalte hain।
Short dipole ke liye, r one approximately r minus a cosine theta ban jaata hai, r two ban jaata hai r plus a cosine theta, aur unka product simply r squared mein collapse ho jaata hai।
Ye isliye hota hai kyunki a, r ke comparison mein itna chhota hai ki tiny correction terms multiply karne ke baad mushkil se matter karte hain।

In approximations ko substitute karke, aur dipole moment p equals two a q use karke, poora expression collapse ho jaata hai V equals one over four pi epsilon zero, times p cosine theta over r squared mein।

Notice karo ye potential one over r squared ki tarah falls off hota hai, single charge ke one over r se faster, exactly kyunki opposite charges bade distance par ek doosre ko nearly cancel kar dete hain।

board_events.text: The instinct that snares students is: equal and opposite, so everything cancels, potential zero and field zero.

segments.text: Here's a trap that N E E T reliably sets, year after year.
Two charges, plus four microcoulombs and minus four microcoulombs, sit zero point two metres apart, exactly at the midpoint — that's where we need both potential and field.
The instinct that snares students is: they're equal and opposite, so everything cancels, potential equals zero and field equals zero.
That instinct is half right, and that's exactly the trap.
Potential, being a scalar, really does add up as k q one over r plus k q two over r, which at the midpoint gives exactly zero — the two contributions genuinely cancel.
So for potential, the cancel-everything instinct was correct — potential truly is zero here.

But field is a vector: the field from the positive charge points away from it, toward the negative charge; the field from the negative charge points toward it, which is also toward the negative charge — both point the same way, so they add.
Speed rule for exam day: potential cancels because it's a scalar with opposite-sign contributions, while field reinforces because both vectors happen to point the same way.
Yahan ek trap hai jo N E E T reliably set karta hai, saal dar saal।
Do charges, plus four microcoulombs aur minus four microcoulombs, zero point two metres apart hain, exactly midpoint par — wahin humein potential aur field dono chahiye।
Wo instinct jo students ko phasa deta hai: 'ye equal and opposite hain, isliye sab cancel ho jaayega, potential zero aur field bhi zero।'
Wo instinct half right hai, aur yahi exactly trap hai।
Potential, scalar hone ki wajah se, really add hota hai k q one over r plus k q two over r ke roop mein, jo midpoint par exactly zero deta hai — dono contributions genuinely cancel ho jaate hain।
Toh potential ke liye, wo cancel-everything instinct correct tha — potential truly zero hai yahan।

Lekin field ek vector hai: positive charge se field usse door point karta hai, negative charge ki taraf; negative charge se field uski taraf point karta hai, jo bhi negative charge ki taraf hi hai — dono fields exact same direction mein point karte hain, isliye wo add hote hain।

Exam day ke liye speed rule: potential cancel hota hai kyunki wo scalar hai opposite-sign contributions ke saath, jabki field reinforce hota hai kyunki dono vectors same direction mein point karte hain।

sections.title: Pitfalls: V and E ask different questions

board_events.text: Common pitfalls in potential and equipotential surfaces
V equals zero therefore E equals zero, and its reverse, are both wrong — evaluate each separately.
Midpoint of two equal and opposite charges: V is zero, E is not. Midpoint of two equal like charges: E is zero, V is not.
Forgetting potential is a scalar — students drag in angles and components as if adding fields.
Just add k q i over r i terms with their signs — it's a one-line algebraic sum.
Dropping the minus sign in E equals minus dV by dr flips your field direction entirely.
The sign tells you the field points downhill toward lower potential; without it, you'd point uphill by mistake.
Any path along an equipotential surface costs exactly zero work, full stop, no exceptions.
Pro-tip: for a symmetric point, compare distances with a ratio, and run a sign check — positive charges raise potential, negative charges lower it.

segments.text: Let's consolidate the traps this subtopic sets, so you walk into the exam already immune to them.
The biggest one: assuming V equals zero means E equals zero, or the reverse. These are independent questions, and you must evaluate each one on its own.
At the midpoint of two equal and opposite charges, V is zero but E is not; at the midpoint of two equal like charges, E is zero but V is not.
The second trap is forgetting that potential is a scalar. Students drag in angles and components as if they were adding vector fields.
Don't do that. Just add up k q i over r i terms, each with its own sign — it really is a one-line algebraic sum, nothing more.
Third: dropping the minus sign in E equals minus d V by d r. That single sign flips your field direction completely.
The sign tells you the field points downhill, toward lower potential. Lose it, and you'll point your answer uphill by mistake, every time.
Fourth: any path you take along an equipotential surface costs exactly zero work, full stop, with no exceptions for the shape of the path.

<whisper> Pro-tip for speed: for a symmetric point, compare distances using a ratio instead of recomputing k every time, and always run a sign check — positive charges raise potential, negative charges lower it.
Chalo un traps ko consolidate karte hain jo ye subtopic set karta hai, taaki tum exam mein already immune ho kar jao।
Sabse bada trap: assume karna ki V equals zero ka matlab E equals zero, ya reverse। Ye independent questions hain, aur har ek ko apne aap evaluate karna zaroori hai।
Do equal and opposite charges ke midpoint par, V zero hai lekin E nahi; do equal like charges ke midpoint par, E zero hai lekin V nahi।
Doosra trap ye bhoolna hai ki potential ek scalar hai। Students angles aur components drag kar lete hain jaise wo vector fields add kar rahe ho।
Aisa mat karo। Sirf k q i over r i terms add karo, har ek apne sign ke saath — ye really ek one-line algebraic sum hai, kuch aur nahi।
Teesra: E equals minus d V by d r mein minus sign drop kar dena। Wo single sign tumhari field direction poori tarah flip kar deta hai।
Wo sign batata hai ki field downhill point karta hai, lower potential ki taraf। Use lose karo, aur tum apna answer uphill point kar dete ho mistake se, har baar।

sections.title: Potential energy — the cost of assembling a configuration

board_events.text: Potential energy: the assembly bill
Picture seating a large, quarrelsome joint family for a wedding feast — push two who dislike each other close together and you must actively work to keep them there.
Other relatives are inseparable, wanting to sit together; pulling them apart costs work instead.
The total tension stored in any seating plan depends only on who ends up next to whom, never on the order they walked in.

board_events.latex: U = \text{work to assemble the configuration, each charge brought in slowly from infinity}

board_events.text: Because the electrostatic force is conservative, this work depends only on the final arrangement, never on the path or the order of assembly.
That path independence is what makes potential energy a meaningful single number attached to a configuration at all.

segments.text: Subtopic two turns potential into an actual energy bill for a whole arrangement of charges.
Picture seating a large, quarrelsome joint family for a wedding feast. Push two relatives who can't stand each other close together, and you have to actively work to keep them there.
Other relatives are inseparable — they want to sit together, and you'd have to do work to pull them apart instead.
The total tension stored in any seating plan depends only on who ends up sitting next to whom, never on the order in which they walked in.
Potential energy U is exactly this: the total work an external agent must do to assemble a configuration of charges, bringing each one in slowly from infinity.
Because the electrostatic force is conservative, that work depends only on the final arrangement, never on the path taken or the order of assembly.
That path independence is the whole reason potential energy is a meaningful idea at all — one single number attached to a configuration, not a story about how you got there.
Subtopic two potential ko ek actual energy bill mein badal deta hai poore charge arrangement ke liye।

Socho ek bada, jhagdalu joint family ko wedding feast ke liye seat karna। Do relatives jo ek doosre ko bardaasht nahi kar sakte unhe paas rakho, to tumhe actively work karna padega unhe wahan rakhne ke liye।
Doosre relatives inseparable hote hain — wo saath baithna chahte hain, aur unhe alag karne mein tumhe work karna padega।
Kisi bhi seating plan mein total tension stored sirf isse depend karta hai ki kaun kiske paas end mein baitha hai, na ki wo kis order mein aaye the।
Potential energy U exactly yahi hai: total work jo ek external agent ko karna padta hai charges ka configuration assemble karne mein, har ek ko slowly infinity se laate hue।
Kyunki electrostatic force conservative hai, wo work sirf final arrangement par depend karta hai, kabhi bhi path ya assembly ke order par nahi।
Wo path independence hi poori wajah hai ki potential energy ek meaningful idea hai — ek single number jo configuration se attached hai, koi story nahi ki tum wahan kaise pahunche।

segments.text: The sign of U is not a technicality — it tells you the entire story of whether a system is bound or ready to fly apart.
Look at the two configurations here: unlike charges pulled together sit at negative U, while like charges pushed together sit at positive U.
Bring two like charges together and you push against their mutual repulsion. The external agent does positive work, so U ends up greater than zero.
That system is wound up like a compressed spring — the instant you let go, it flies apart on its own.
Bring two unlike charges together instead, and their attraction does the work for you. The external agent does negative work, so U ends up less than zero.
That system is bound, like money locked in a fixed deposit — you would have to invest energy just to pull it apart.
This single idea explains why every bound system in nature, from an electron circling a proton to a planet circling the Sun, always carries negative potential energy.
U ka sign koi technicality nahi hai — ye poori story batata hai ki system bound hai ya fly apart hone ke liye ready hai।
Yahan do configurations dekho: unlike charges jo saath khinche gaye hain negative U par baithte hain, jabki like charges jo saath push kiye gaye hain positive U par baithte hain।
Do like charges ko saath lao aur tum unki mutual repulsion ke against push karte ho। External agent positive work karta hai, isliye U zero se zyada ho jaata hai।
Wo system compressed spring ki tarah wound up hota hai — jaise hi tum chhodte ho, wo apne aap fly apart ho jaata hai।
Iske jagah do unlike charges ko saath lao, aur unki attraction tumhare liye work kar deti hai। External agent negative work karta hai, isliye U zero se kam ho jaata hai।
Wo system bound hota hai, jaise fixed deposit mein locked money — use alag karne ke liye tumhe energy invest karni padegi।
Yehi single idea explain karta hai ki nature mein har bound system, electron ka proton ke around circle karna ho ya planet ka Sun ke around, hamesha negative potential energy carry karta hai।

sections.title: Energy conservation and the work-energy sign convention

board_events.text: Energy bookkeeping: K plus U stays constant
Release a charge and watch U convert into K — it speeds up exactly as much as potential energy falls.
When the field does positive work on a charge, letting it fall downhill in energy, U decreases.
When an external agent does positive work dragging the charge uphill against the field, U increases instead.
Keep a firm grip on who is doing the work, and the sign sorts itself out every time.

segments.text: One equation solves a huge fraction of exam problems in this subtopic.
If only electrostatic forces act, kinetic energy plus potential energy stays exactly constant: K initial plus U initial equals K final plus U final.
Release a charge and watch potential energy convert straight into kinetic energy — it speeds up exactly as much as U falls.
The signed relation underneath all of this is: work done by the field equals minus the change in U.
When the field does positive work on a charge, letting it fall downhill in energy the way a stone drops under gravity, U decreases.
The mirror image is work done by an external agent, which equals plus the change in U.
When an external agent does positive work dragging a charge uphill against the field, U increases instead.
Keep a firm grip on exactly who is doing the work in any given problem, and the sign of every term sorts itself out, every single time.
Ek equation is subtopic ke exam problems ka bada hissa solve kar deta hai।
Agar sirf electrostatic forces act kar rahe hain, to kinetic energy plus potential energy exactly constant rehta hai: K initial plus U initial equals K final plus U final.
Ek charge ko release karo aur dekho potential energy seedhe kinetic energy mein convert hoti hai — wo exactly usi rate se speed up hoti hai jitna U falls hota hai।
Is sab ke peeche wo signed relation hai: field dwara kiya gaya work equals minus the change in U.
Jab field kisi charge par positive work karta hai, use energy mein downhill fall karne deta hai jaise gravity ke under ek stone drop hota hai, U decrease hota hai।
Iska mirror image hai external agent dwara kiya gaya work, jo equals plus the change in U.
Jab external agent positive work karta hai charge ko uphill khinch kar field ke against, U increase ho jaata hai instead.
Kisi bhi problem mein exactly kaun work kar raha hai, usko firmly grip karo, aur har term ka sign apne aap sort ho jaata hai, har single baar।

sections.title: Formula toolkit: potential energy of charge systems

board_events.text: Formula toolkit: potential energy
For a system of n charges, sum over all distinct pairs, with a factor of one half if summing over every charge instead.
The number of distinct pairs for n charges is n times n minus one, all over two.
This bridge matters: U in joules describes the charge-plus-field system, while V in volts is purely a property of the point.

board_events.latex: U = q_1 V(\vec r_1) + q_2 V(\vec r_2) + \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q_1 q_2}{r_{12}}

board_events.text: That last formula has three pieces: each charge's energy in the external field, plus the familiar mutual term between the two charges.

segments.text: Let's collect the formulas for potential energy in one place.
For two point charges, U equals one over four pi epsilon zero, times q one q two over r one two.
For a system of n charges, sum over every distinct pair, or equivalently take one half of the sum over each charge times the potential at its own location.
That equivalent form, one half times the sum of q i V i, prevents double counting each pair.
The number of distinct pairs for n charges is n times n minus one, divided by two — three pairs for three charges, six for four.
For a single charge sitting in an existing external potential, U equals q times V — the clean bridge between joules and volts.
That bridge matters: U in joules describes the charge-plus-field system, while V in volts is purely a property of the point.
For two charges together in an external field, add each one's individual energy in that field to their own mutual interaction energy.
That last formula has three pieces: each charge's energy in the external field, plus the familiar mutual term between the two charges themselves.
Chalo potential energy ke formulas ek jagah collect karte hain।
Do point charges ke liye, U equals one over four pi epsilon zero, times q one q two over r one two.
N charges ke system ke liye, har distinct pair par sum karo, ya equivalently one half lo sum of q i V i ka, har charge ki apni location par potential ke saath।
Wo equivalent form, one half times the sum of q i V i, har pair ko double count hone se rokta hai।
N charges ke liye distinct pairs ki number hoti hai n times n minus one, divided by two — three pairs three charges ke liye, six four charges ke liye।
Ek single charge ke liye jo existing external potential mein baitha hai, U equals q times V — clean bridge joules aur volts ke beech।
Wo bridge important hai: U joules mein charge-plus-field system describe karta hai, jabki V volts mein purely point ki property hai।
External field mein saath do charges ke liye, har ek ki individual energy us field mein add karo unki apni mutual interaction energy mein।
Us last formula ke teen pieces hain: har charge ki energy external field mein, plus wo familiar mutual term dono charges ke beech।

sections.title: Dipole torque and potential energy in a uniform field — formulas

board_events.text: Dipole in a uniform field: torque and energy
Theta is the angle between the dipole moment and the field.
Stable equilibrium sits at theta equals zero, where U is minimum, at minus p E.
Unstable equilibrium sits at theta equals one hundred eighty degrees, U maximum at plus p E; the reference U equals zero is at theta equals ninety degrees.
One electron-volt equals one point six times ten to the minus nineteen joules, the energy one electron gains crossing one volt.

segments.text: Two formulas govern a dipole sitting in a uniform external field: torque and potential energy.
The torque is p cross E, with magnitude p E sine theta, where theta is the angle between the dipole moment and the field.
The potential energy is U of theta equals minus p dot E, or minus p E cosine theta.
That angle theta always means the same thing: the angle between the dipole's moment vector and the external field.
Stable equilibrium sits at theta equal to zero, where U reaches its minimum value of minus p E — the dipole's preferred resting position.
Unstable equilibrium sits at theta equal to one hundred eighty degrees, where U reaches its maximum of plus p E; by convention, we set U equal to zero at theta equal to ninety degrees.
The same energy bookkeeping from before still applies: work by the field equals minus delta U, work by an external agent equals plus delta U, and K plus U stays constant.
One handy unit worth knowing: one electron-volt equals one point six times ten to the minus nineteen joules, the energy a single electron gains crossing a potential of one volt.
Do formulas govern karte hain ek dipole ko jo uniform external field mein baitha hai: torque aur potential energy।
Torque hota hai p cross E, magnitude p E sine theta ke saath, jahan theta dipole moment aur field ke beech ka angle hai।
Potential energy hoti hai U of theta equals minus p dot E, ya minus p E cosine theta.
Wo angle theta hamesha same cheez matlab hota hai: dipole ke moment vector aur external field ke beech ka angle।
Stable equilibrium theta equal to zero par baithta hai, jahan U apna minimum value reach karta hai minus p E ka — dipole ki preferred resting position।

Unstable equilibrium theta equal to one hundred eighty degrees par baithta hai, jahan U apna maximum plus p E reach karta hai; by convention, hum U equal to zero set karte hain theta equal to ninety degrees par।
Wahi purani energy bookkeeping abhi bhi apply hoti hai: field dwara work equals minus delta U, external agent dwara work equals plus delta U, aur K plus U constant rehta hai।
Ek handy unit jaanna zaroori hai: one electron-volt equals one point six times ten to the minus nineteen joules, wo energy jo ek single electron gain karta hai one volt cross karne mein।

sections.title: Deriving the potential energy of a two-charge system

board_events.text: Derivation: potential energy of two point charges
Assemble the system on an empty stage, taking U equal to zero when the charges are infinitely far apart, bringing each in infinitely slowly.
Step one: bring in q one. The stage is empty, so there is no field and no force to fight — work done is zero.
Step two: bring in q two, to a point where q one already produces this potential.
The work done bringing q two to a point of existing potential V one is, by definition, q two times V one.
Bringing q two in first instead gives the identical answer, confirming the result never depends on assembly order.

segments.text: Let's derive the two-charge potential energy formula from a genuinely empty stage.
Take U equal to zero when the charges are infinitely far apart, and bring each one in infinitely slowly, so no kinetic energy sneaks in.
Step one: bring in q one. The stage is completely empty at this point, so there is no field and nothing to fight against — the work done is exactly zero.
Now q one sits at the origin, producing a potential at the destination point equal to one over four pi epsilon zero, times q one over r one two.
Step two: bring in q two, to that exact point where q one's potential already exists.
By the very definition of potential, the work to bring q two there is q two times that potential, giving U equals one over four pi epsilon zero, times q one q two over r one two.
That's the key step: work done in bringing a charge to a point of existing potential is always that charge times the potential.
One sanity check: bringing q two in first and q one second gives the exact same answer, confirming this result never depends on the order of assembly.
Chalo two-charge potential energy formula ko ek genuinely empty stage se derive karte hain।
U equal to zero lo jab charges infinitely far apart hain, aur har ek ko infinitely slowly laao, taaki koi kinetic energy na ghuse।
Step one: q one ko laao। Stage abhi completely empty hai, isliye koi field nahi aur kuch fight karne ke liye nahi hai — work done exactly zero hota hai।
Ab q one origin par baitha hai, destination point par ek potential produce karta hai equal to one over four pi epsilon zero, times q one over r one two.
Step two: q two ko laao, exactly wahan jahan q one ka potential already exist karta hai।
Potential ki very definition se, q two ko wahan laane mein work hota hai q two times wo potential, jo deta hai U equals one over four pi epsilon zero, times q one q two over r one two.
Yahi key step hai: existing potential ke point tak charge laane mein hua work hamesha wo charge times potential hota hai।
Ek sanity check: q two ko pehle aur q one ko doosra laane se exactly same answer milta hai, jo confirm karta hai ki ye result kabhi assembly ke order par depend nahi karta।

segments.text: Let's derive where the dipole's energy formula, U equals minus p dot E, actually comes from.
Here's the setup: a short dipole of moment p sits inclined at angle theta inside a uniform field, with a torque trying to align it.
In a uniform field, the two equal-and-opposite forces on plus q and minus q cancel exactly, so there is no net force at all — only this torque.
That torque has magnitude p E sine theta.
Now imagine an external agent applying just enough torque to rotate the dipole quasi-statically, without any angular acceleration, from an initial angle theta zero to a final angle theta one.
The work done against the field's torque is the integral of tau d theta, which works out to p E times cosine theta zero minus cosine theta one.
Rotating through a small angle against torque costs work tau d theta, exactly the rotational twin of force times distance — and this stored work becomes the change in potential energy.

At ninety degrees the dipole is neither helped nor hindered by the field, which is exactly why that angle makes such a natural, clean reference point.

Field ke torque ke against kiya gaya work hota hai integral of tau d theta, jo nikal ke aata hai p E times cosine theta zero minus cosine theta one.
Torque ke against small angle rotate karna work leta hai tau d theta, exactly rotational twin force times distance ka — aur ye stored work potential energy ka change ban jaata hai।

Ninety degrees par dipole na field se help hota hai na hinder, aur yahi exactly wajah hai ki wo angle ek natural, clean reference point banta hai।

Arithmetic work through karne se milta hai minus zero point two two five joules.

sections.title: NEET speed trap: one over r, not one over r squared

board_events.text: NEET speed trap: energy goes as one over r, not one over r squared
Two charges, each plus four microcoulombs, sit zero point two metres apart; find the potential energy of the pair.
The trap: under pressure, students reach for the force habit and divide by r squared instead of r.
Potential energy scales as one over r, so the correct division is by zero point two, not by its square.
That seductive wrong answer is exactly five times too big, because zero point two squared is zero point zero four instead of zero point two.
Speed rule: potential energy goes as one over r; if your exponent matches the force law, you've slipped.

segments.text: Here's a trap N E E T reuses constantly, hiding inside a two-line calculation.
Two charges, each plus four microcoulombs, sit zero point two metres apart. Find the potential energy of the pair.
Under exam pressure, the force-and-field habit kicks in, and students divide by r squared instead of r — that's the trap hiding in plain sight.
The correct calculation is nine times ten to the ninth, times four microcoulombs squared, divided by zero point two, which gives zero point seven two joules.
Potential energy scales as one over r, not one over r squared — that division by zero point two, not by its square, is the whole ballgame here.
The seductive wrong answer comes from dividing by zero point two squared instead, giving three point six joules.
That wrong answer is exactly five times too big, because zero point two squared is zero point zero four, not zero point two.
Speed rule for exam day: potential energy goes as one over r; if your exponent matches the force law's one over r squared, you have slipped.
Yahan ek trap hai jo N E E T constantly reuse karta hai, ek two-line calculation ke andar chhupa hua।
Do charges, har ek plus four microcoulombs, zero point two metres apart baithe hain। Pair ki potential energy find karo।
Exam pressure mein, force-and-field wali habit kick in hoti hai, aur students r squared se divide kar dete hain r ke jagah — yahi trap hai plain sight mein chhupa hua।
Correct calculation hai nine times ten to the ninth, times four microcoulombs squared, divided by zero point two, jo deta hai zero point seven two joules.
Potential energy one over r ki tarah scale karti hai, one over r squared ki tarah nahi — wo division by zero point two, uske square se nahi, yahi poora ballgame hai yahan।
Wo seductive wrong answer aata hai zero point two squared se divide karne se, jo deta hai three point six joules.
Wo wrong answer exactly five times too big hai, kyunki zero point two squared zero point zero four hai, zero point two nahi।
Exam day ke liye speed rule: potential energy one over r ki tarah jaati hai; agar tumhara exponent force law ke one over r squared se match kar jaaye, to tum slip ho gaye ho।

sections.title: JEE Main: released charge, conservation of energy

board_events.text: JEE Main: released charge, conservation of energy
Charge q one, plus five microcoulombs, is fixed. Charge q two, plus two microcoulombs, mass five grams, is released from rest zero point one metres away.
The two like charges repel, so q two accelerates outward, converting electrostatic potential energy into kinetic energy.
At infinity, U final is zero, and the charge started from rest, so K initial is zero — every joule of initial potential energy becomes kinetic.
Two ideas stitched together here: the one-over-r potential energy law, then straightforward conservation of mechanical energy.

segments.text: This example stitches two ideas together: the potential energy formula, and conservation of energy.
Charge q one, plus five microcoulombs, stays fixed in place. Charge q two, plus two microcoulombs with a mass of five grams, is released from rest zero point one metres away.
These two like charges repel each other, so q two accelerates outward, and electrostatic potential energy converts steadily into kinetic energy as it moves.
Apply conservation of mechanical energy between the starting point and a point very far away: U initial plus K initial equals U final plus K final.
The initial potential energy is nine times ten to the ninth, times five microcoulombs times two microcoulombs, over zero point one metres, which comes to zero point nine zero joules.
Far away, U final is essentially zero, and since the charge started from rest, K initial is zero too — so every joule of that initial potential energy becomes kinetic energy.
Solving for speed from one half m v squared equals zero point nine zero joules gives v approximately equal to nineteen metres per second.
Notice the two ideas stitched together: first the one-over-r potential energy law, then plain conservation of mechanical energy to finish the job.
Ye example do ideas ko saath stitch karta hai: potential energy formula, aur conservation of energy।
Charge q one, plus five microcoulombs, fixed rehta hai apni jagah। Charge q two, plus two microcoulombs, mass five grams, rest se release hota hai zero point one metres door।
Ye do like charges ek doosre ko repel karte hain, isliye q two outward accelerate karta hai, aur electrostatic potential energy steadily kinetic energy mein convert hoti hai jaise wo move karta hai।
Starting point aur bahut door ke point ke beech conservation of mechanical energy apply karo: U initial plus K initial equals U final plus K final.
Initial potential energy hai nine times ten to the ninth, times five microcoulombs times two microcoulombs, over zero point one metres, jo aata hai zero point nine zero joules.
Bahut door, U final essentially zero hai, aur kyunki charge rest se start hua tha, K initial bhi zero hai — isliye har joule of initial potential energy kinetic energy ban jaata hai।
One half m v squared equals zero point nine zero joules se speed solve karne se milta hai v approximately equal to nineteen metres per second.

segments.text: This one takes the dipole energy formula and puts it through rotational motion.

Picture a dipole of moment four times ten to the minus ninth coulomb metre, with moment of inertia one times ten to the minus six kilogram metre squared, sitting in a field of two times ten to the fourth newtons per coulomb.
It is released from rest at theta equal to ninety degrees, perpendicular to the field, and we want its angular speed once it becomes aligned at theta equal to zero.
Only the field's torque does any work here, so rotational mechanical energy is conserved from start to finish, and the drop in potential energy has to reappear entirely as rotational kinetic energy.

Physically, the dipole swings toward alignment exactly the way a released pendulum swings to its lowest point — minimum potential energy, maximum kinetic energy.

sections.title: Pitfalls: one over r, sign slips, and pair-counting

board_events.text: Common pitfalls in potential energy
Using one over r squared instead of one over r for energy. Force and field go as one over r squared; potential and potential energy go as one over r.
Tattoo this distinction on your formula sheet — it's the single most common arithmetic disaster in this subtopic.
Sign slips. Always plug charges in with their own signs.
Quick sanity check: like charges give U greater than zero, unlike charges give U less than zero. If your final sign disagrees, hunt for the error.
Confusing U, V, and E: E is force per charge, a vector; V is energy per charge at a point, a scalar; U is the energy of a charge-in-field or a whole system. U equals qV is the bridge.
Pair-counting errors in multi-charge systems: a system of n charges has n times n minus one over two distinct pairs — miss one and your total is wrong.
Dipole min-max confusion: stable rest is theta equal to zero, where U is minimum at minus p E; theta equal to one hundred eighty degrees is unstable, where U is maximum at plus p E.
Pro-tip: for released from rest, find the speed, skip forces entirely and go straight to delta K equals minus delta U.

segments.text: Let's consolidate the traps this subtopic sets, one after another.
The single most common arithmetic disaster: using one over r squared instead of one over r for energy. Force and field go as one over r squared; potential and potential energy go as one over r.
Tattoo that distinction onto your formula sheet if you have to — it costs marks every single exam cycle.
Second: sign slips. Always plug charges in with their own signs, never their magnitudes alone.
Run a quick sanity check after every calculation: like charges should give U greater than zero, unlike charges should give U less than zero. If your final sign disagrees, go hunt for the error.

Third: confusing U, V, and E. E is force per charge, a vector; V is energy per charge at a point, a scalar; U is the energy of a charge-in-field or a whole system, and U equals q V is the bridge connecting them.
Fourth: pair-counting errors in multi-charge systems. A system of n charges has n times n minus one, over two, distinct pairs — miss even one pair and your total is wrong.

Fifth: dipole minimum-maximum confusion. Stable rest sits at theta equal to zero, where U is minimum at minus p E; theta equal to one hundred eighty degrees is unstable, where U is maximum at plus p E.
<curious> Pro-tip for speed: whenever you see 'released from rest, find the speed,' skip forces entirely and jump straight to delta K equals minus delta U — it's almost always faster.
Chalo ek ke baad ek is subtopic ke traps ko consolidate karte hain।

Sabse common arithmetic disaster: energy ke liye one over r squared use karna instead of one over r. Force aur field one over r squared ki tarah jaate hain; potential aur potential energy one over r ki tarah jaate hain।
Agar zaroorat pade to ye distinction apne formula sheet par tattoo kar lo — ye har exam cycle mein marks costs karta hai।
Doosra: sign slips. Charges ko hamesha unke apne signs ke saath plug karo, sirf magnitudes ke saath nahi।

Har calculation ke baad ek quick sanity check chalao: like charges ko U zero se zyada dena chahiye, unlike charges ko U zero se kam dena chahiye। Agar final sign disagree kare, to jaake error dhoondo।

Teesra: U, V, aur E ko confuse karna। E force per charge hai, ek vector; V energy per charge hai kisi point par, ek scalar; U charge-in-field ya poore system ki energy hai, aur U equals q V hi wo bridge hai jo unhe connect karta hai।
Chautha: multi-charge systems mein pair-counting errors। N charges ke system mein n times n minus one, over two, distinct pairs hote hain — ek bhi pair miss karo aur tumhara total wrong ho jaata hai।

Paanchwa: dipole minimum-maximum confusion। Stable rest theta equal to zero par baithta hai, jahan U minimum hota hai minus p E par; theta equal to one hundred eighty degrees unstable hai, jahan U maximum hota hai plus p E par।

<curious> Speed ke liye pro-tip: jab bhi tum dekho 'released from rest, find the speed,' forces ko poori tarah skip karo aur seedhe jump karo delta K equals minus delta U par — ye almost always faster hota hai।

segments.text: <curious> Think about the overhead water tank on the roof of a house.
Pour in water and the level rises. How fast that level climbs depends on two things: how much water you poured in, and the shape of the tank itself.
A wide tank barely rises for a whole lot of water; a narrow pipe shoots up fast for just a little. Same water in, wildly different level reached.
Now swap water for electric charge, and swap water level for voltage, and what you have is exactly a capacitor.
Capacitance is the measure of that storage capacity: how much charge a conductor system holds per volt of potential it rises to.
A capacitor with large capacitance soaks up a great deal of charge while barely changing its voltage at all. That is the wide tank, in electrical form.
In practice, a capacitor is nothing exotic: just two conductors separated by an insulator. Most simply of all, two parallel metal plates.
Put plus Q on one plate and minus Q on the other. A uniform field appears in the gap, a potential difference builds across it, and the ratio of the two gives you capacitance.
<curious> Ghar ki chhat par lage overhead water tank ke baare mein socho।
Paani daalo aur level rise hota hai। Wo level kitni tezi se chadhta hai, ye do cheezon par depend karta hai: tumne kitna paani daala, aur khud tank ka shape kya hai।

Ab paani ko electric charge se swap karo, aur water level ko voltage se, aur jo bacha wo exactly ek capacitor hai।
Capacitance us storage capacity ka measure hai: ek conductor system kitna charge hold karta hai per volt potential jispar wo rise karta hai।
Bade capacitance wala capacitor bahut saara charge soak kar leta hai apna voltage mushkil se badalte hue। Wahi wide tank hai, electrical form mein।
Practically, capacitor kuch exotic nahi hai: bas do conductors jo ek insulator se separated hain। Sabse simple form mein, do parallel metal plates।
Ek plate par plus Q rakho aur doosri par minus Q। Gap mein ek uniform field appear hota hai, uske across ek potential difference build hota hai, aur dono ka ratio tumhe capacitance de deta hai।

sections.title: Capacitance is geometry alone — not charge, not voltage

board_events.text: Capacitance depends only on geometry
Capacitance is a property of geometry alone — plate area, separation, and what fills the gap.
It does not depend on how much charge you have stored, nor on what voltage you have applied.
Pouring more water into a tank does not widen the tank; charging a capacitor more does not change its capacitance.

board_events.latex: C = \frac{Q}{V} \quad \text{stays fixed because } Q \text{ and } V \text{ rise together}

board_events.text: So if a problem tells you the capacitance changed, something geometric or dielectric changed — never merely the charge or voltage.
The S I unit is the farad, one coulomb per volt, though practical capacitors run in picofarads, nanofarads, and microfarads.

segments.text: Here is the most important and most counterintuitive fact in this entire subtopic.
Capacitance is a property of geometry alone. Plate area, plate separation, and whatever material fills the gap. That is the complete list.
It does not depend on how much charge you happen to have stored, and it does not depend on what voltage you happen to have applied.
Go back to the tank: pouring in more water does not widen the tank. In exactly the same way, charging a capacitor more does not change its capacitance one bit.
The ratio Q over V stays fixed for a simple reason: charge and voltage rise in perfect lockstep. Double the charge and you exactly double the voltage.
So here is your diagnostic: if a problem implies capacitance has changed, then something geometric or something about the dielectric must have changed. Never merely the charge or the voltage.
The S I unit is the farad, defined as one coulomb per volt. A farad is enormous in practice, so real capacitors are rated in picofarads, nanofarads, and microfarads.
Yahan is poore subtopic ka sabse important aur sabse counterintuitive fact hai।
Capacitance sirf geometry ki property hai। Plate area, plate separation, aur jo bhi material gap ko fill karta hai। Bas, poori list yahi hai।
Ye is par depend nahi karta ki tumne kitna charge store kiya hai, aur na hi is par ki tumne kaunsa voltage apply kiya hai।
Tank par wapas jao: zyada paani daalne se tank chauda nahi hota। Bilkul usi tarah, capacitor ko zyada charge karne se uska capacitance zara bhi nahi badalta।
Q over V ka ratio ek simple reason se fixed rehta hai: charge aur voltage perfect lockstep mein rise karte hain। Charge double karo aur voltage bhi exactly double ho jaata hai।
Toh yahan tumhara diagnostic hai: agar koi problem imply kare ki capacitance badal gaya, to kuch geometric ya dielectric ke baare mein kuch badla hoga। Kabhi sirf charge ya voltage nahi।
S I unit farad hai, jo define hota hai one coulomb per volt। Practically farad bahut bada hai, isliye real capacitors picofarads, nanofarads, aur microfarads mein rated hote hain।

K is always at least one; a dielectric can only ever increase capacitance, never decrease it.

segments.text: Now slide an insulating slab into the gap, and something genuinely useful happens.
Take glass, mica, or plastic. The slab cannot conduct at all, but its molecules polarise: they stretch or rotate so their positive ends face the negative plate.
Picture a parade of tiny compass needles, every one of them swinging around to point the same way. That is what polarisation looks like at the molecular level.
These lined-up charges create their own field, and crucially it opposes the original field. So the net field inside the gap weakens.
The field falls by a factor K, the dielectric constant. Weaker field means lower voltage for the same charge, which means more capacitance — capacitance is multiplied by K.
K is always at least one, equal to one for vacuum and effectively for air. So a dielectric can only ever increase capacitance, never decrease it.
One caution before we go further: that clean relation, E equals E-naught over K, assumes the dielectric completely fills the gap. Partial fills have to be analysed slab by slab.

And every real dielectric carries a second property: dielectric strength, the maximum field it can withstand before it breaks down and starts conducting. That is a completely different quantity from K.
Ab gap mein ek insulating slab slide karo, aur kuch genuinely useful hota hai।

Glass, mica, ya plastic lo। Wo slab bilkul conduct nahi kar sakta, lekin uske molecules polarise ho jaate hain: wo stretch ya rotate karte hain taaki unke positive ends negative plate ki taraf face karein।
Socho chhote compass needles ki ek parade, har ek ghoom kar same direction mein point kar rahi hai। Molecular level par polarisation aisa hi dikhta hai।
Ye lined-up charges apna khud ka field create karte hain, aur crucially wo original field ka opposition karta hai। Isliye gap ke andar net field weak ho jaata hai।

Field ek factor K se gir jaata hai, jise dielectric constant kehte hain। Weaker field ka matlab same charge ke liye lower voltage, jiska matlab zyada capacitance — capacitance K se multiply ho jaata hai।
K hamesha kam se kam one hota hai, vacuum ke liye one aur effectively air ke liye bhi। Isliye dielectric sirf capacitance badha sakta hai, kabhi ghata nahi sakta।
Aage badhne se pehle ek caution: wo clean relation, E equals E-naught over K, assume karta hai ki dielectric poora gap fill karta hai। Partial fills ko slab by slab analyse karna padta hai।

Aur har real dielectric ki ek doosri property hoti hai: dielectric strength, wo maximum field jo wo sah sakta hai break down hone aur conduct karna shuru karne se pehle। Ye K se bilkul alag quantity hai।

segments.text: <whisper> If you remember one thing from this subtopic, make it this fork. It decides every dielectric problem you will ever face.
Every dielectric-insertion question branches at exactly one point: is the battery still connected, or has it been removed?
If the battery is disconnected, the charge on the plates is trapped, with nowhere to go. So Q is king. It stays constant, and everything else adjusts around it.
In that branch, voltage, field, and stored energy all fall by the factor K, because capacitance rose by K while the charge stayed locked in place.
If the battery is still connected, it clamps the voltage at its own E M F. Now V is king. It stays constant instead, and charge flows in or out of the battery as needed.
In that branch, charge and stored energy both rise by the factor K, while the field in the gap stays completely unchanged, since V and d both stayed the same.
Get this fork right and dielectric questions become pure bookkeeping. Get it wrong and every downstream number is wrong. Decide it first, every single time, before touching a formula.
<whisper> Agar is subtopic se ek cheez yaad rakhni hai, to ye fork yaad rakho। Ye har dielectric problem decide karta hai jo tumhe kabhi milegi।
Har dielectric-insertion question exactly ek point par branch hota hai: kya battery abhi bhi connected hai, ya use hata diya gaya hai?
Agar battery disconnected hai, to plates par charge trapped hai, jaane ki koi jagah nahi। Isliye Q is king. Wo constant rehta hai, aur baaki sab uske around adjust hota hai।
Us branch mein, voltage, field, aur stored energy sab factor K se gir jaate hain, kyunki capacitance K se badha jabki charge apni jagah locked raha।

Agar battery abhi bhi connected hai, to wo voltage ko apne E M F par clamp kar deti hai। Ab V is king. Wo constant rehta hai, aur charge zaroorat ke hisaab se battery se andar ya bahar flow karta hai।
Us branch mein, charge aur stored energy dono factor K se rise karte hain, jabki gap mein field bilkul unchanged rehta hai, kyunki V aur d dono same rahe।

Is fork ko sahi karo aur dielectric questions pure bookkeeping ban jaate hain। Galat karo aur har downstream number galat ho jaata hai। Isse pehle decide karo, har single baar, formula touch karne se pehle।

sections.title: Formula toolkit: capacitance and the parallel plate

board_events.text: Formula toolkit: capacitance and parallel plates
Here sigma is the surface charge density, Q over A, and V equals E d holds because the field between the plates is uniform.
A is the plate area in square metres, d is the separation in metres, and K is dimensionless and at least one.

segments.text: Let's collect the core capacitance formulas in one place.
The definition of capacitance: Q over V, where Q is the magnitude of charge on each plate and V is the potential difference across them.
Dimensionally, capacitance works out to M to the minus one, L to the minus two, T to the fourth, A squared.
Between parallel plates, the field is sigma over epsilon zero, which is Q over epsilon zero A, and the potential difference is simply E times d.
Here sigma is the surface charge density, Q over A, and the relation V equals E d holds precisely because the field between the plates is uniform.
For a parallel plate capacitor in vacuum or air, capacitance is epsilon zero A over d.
Fill that gap with a dielectric of constant K and capacitance becomes K epsilon zero A over d, which is simply K times the vacuum value.
In both formulas, A is the plate area in square metres, d is the separation in metres, and K is dimensionless and never less than one.
Chalo core capacitance formulas ek jagah collect karte hain।
Capacitance ki definition: Q over V, jahan Q har plate par charge ka magnitude hai aur V unke across potential difference hai।
Dimensionally, capacitance nikal ke aata hai M to the minus one, L to the minus two, T to the fourth, A squared।
Parallel plates ke beech, field hota hai sigma over epsilon zero, jo Q over epsilon zero A hai, aur potential difference simply E times d hota hai।
Yahan sigma surface charge density hai, Q over A, aur V equals E d wala relation exactly isliye hold karta hai kyunki plates ke beech field uniform hai।
Vacuum ya air mein parallel plate capacitor ke liye, capacitance hota hai epsilon zero A over d.
Us gap ko constant K wale dielectric se fill karo aur capacitance ban jaata hai K epsilon zero A over d, jo simply K times vacuum value hai।
Dono formulas mein, A plate area hai square metres mein, d separation hai metres mein, aur K dimensionless hai aur kabhi one se kam nahi hota।

sections.title: Formula toolkit: stored energy and energy density

board_events.text: Energy stored in a capacitor
They are algebraically identical, but choosing the right one makes dielectric problems dramatically easier.
Use Q squared over two C when charge is fixed; use one half C V squared when voltage is fixed.
Pick the form matching your fixed quantity and the K-scaling falls out cleanly; pick the wrong one and it gets buried in algebra.
This tells you something physically deep: the energy is not sitting on the plates, it is stored in the field filling the gap.
And a useful fact: when charging through a battery, exactly half the battery's energy is always lost as heat.

segments.text: Three equivalent forms describe the energy stored in a charged capacitor.
Energy equals one half C V squared, which also equals Q squared over two C, which also equals one half Q V. All three are the same number.
They are algebraically identical, so any one of them gives the right answer. But choosing the right one makes dielectric problems dramatically easier.
Use Q squared over two C when the charge is fixed, meaning the battery was disconnected. Use one half C V squared when the voltage is fixed, meaning the battery is still connected.
Pick the form that matches your fixed quantity, and the way everything scales with K falls out in one line. Pick the wrong one and that scaling gets buried under unnecessary algebra.
The energy density, meaning energy per unit volume of field, is one half epsilon zero E squared.
This formula tells you something physically deep. The energy is not sitting on the plates at all. It is stored in the electric field that fills the gap between them.
One more fact worth banking: when you charge a capacitor through a battery, exactly half the energy the battery supplies is always lost as heat, regardless of the circuit resistance.
Teen equivalent forms charged capacitor mein stored energy ko describe karte hain।
Energy equals one half C V squared, jo Q squared over two C ke bhi barabar hai, jo one half Q V ke bhi barabar hai। Teenon same number hain।
Wo algebraically identical hain, isliye koi bhi ek sahi answer dega। Lekin sahi wala choose karna dielectric problems ko dramatically easier bana deta hai।
Q squared over two C use karo jab charge fixed ho, matlab battery disconnect ho gayi ho। One half C V squared use karo jab voltage fixed ho, matlab battery abhi bhi connected ho।

Wo form choose karo jo tumhari fixed quantity se match kare, aur K ke saath sab kaise scale hota hai wo ek line mein nikal aayega। Galat wala choose karo aur wo scaling unnecessary algebra ke neeche dab jaayega।
Energy density, matlab field ke per unit volume energy, hoti hai one half epsilon zero E squared.
Ye formula tumhe kuch physically deep batata hai। Energy plates par bilkul nahi baithi hai। Wo us electric field mein stored hai jo unke beech gap ko fill karta hai।

Ek aur fact bank karne layak: jab tum battery se capacitor charge karte ho, battery jo energy supply karti hai uska exactly half hamesha heat ke roop mein lost ho jaata hai, chahe circuit resistance kuch bhi ho।
