board_events.text: Charge sloshes from the higher-potential capacitor to the lower one until they settle at a common potential.
Total charge is conserved throughout: whatever leaves one capacitor arrives at the other.
But total energy is not conserved — some is always lost as heat in the wires and a little radiation.
The loss is unavoidable and vanishes only in the special case where both capacitors already sat at the same voltage.
These results assume the two capacitors are joined like plate to like plate, positive to positive, unless stated otherwise.

segments.text: There is a third situation worth flagging now, because it surprises students every single year.
Take two capacitors that are already charged, sitting at different potentials, and join them together.
Charge immediately sloshes from the higher-potential capacitor across to the lower one, and it keeps flowing until both settle at one single common potential.
Total charge is conserved throughout this process. Whatever leaves one capacitor arrives at the other — nothing is created and nothing vanishes.
But here is the part that catches people out: total energy is not conserved. Some of it is always lost, as heat in the connecting wires and a little as radiation.
That loss is unavoidable, and it vanishes only in the one special case where both capacitors already happened to sit at exactly the same voltage — in which case no charge flows at all.
One assumption worth stating: these results assume the two capacitors are joined like plate to like plate, positive terminal to positive terminal, unless a problem tells you otherwise.
Ek teesri situation hai jo abhi flag karne layak hai, kyunki ye har saal students ko surprise karti hai।
Do capacitors lo jo already charged hain, alag alag potentials par baithe hain, aur unhe saath jod do।
Charge turant higher-potential capacitor se lower wale ki taraf slosh karta hai, aur tab tak flow karta rehta hai jab tak dono ek single common potential par settle na ho jaayein।
Is poore process mein total charge conserved rehta hai। Jo bhi ek capacitor se jaata hai wo doosre par pahunchta hai — kuch create nahi hota aur kuch gaayab nahi hota।
Lekin yahi wo hissa hai jo logon ko pakad leta hai: total energy conserved nahi hoti। Uska kuch hissa hamesha lost hota hai, connecting wires mein heat ke roop mein aur thoda radiation ke roop mein।
Wo loss unavoidable hai, aur wo sirf us ek special case mein vanish hota hai jahan dono capacitors already exactly same voltage par baithe the — jismein koi charge flow hi nahi karta।
Ek assumption batane layak: ye results assume karte hain ki dono capacitors like plate to like plate jode gaye hain, positive terminal se positive terminal, jab tak koi problem kuch aur na bataye।

sections.title: Formula toolkit: series and parallel combinations

board_events.text: Formula toolkit: series and parallel
In series the charge is common: Q equals C one V one equals C two V two, and the total voltage is the sum of the individual drops.

board_events.latex: C_{\text{parallel}} = C_1 + C_2 + \cdots + C_n, \qquad C_{\text{parallel}} = nC \quad (n \text{ equal})

board_events.text: In parallel the voltage is common, the total charge is the sum, and each capacitor's charge is its own C times V.
Sanity checks: series must come out below the smallest member, parallel must come out above the largest.
For n equal capacitors, the ratio between the parallel and series values is exactly n squared.

segments.text: Let's collect the combination formulas in one place.
For capacitors in series, the reciprocal of the equivalent capacitance is the sum of the individual reciprocals.
For just two capacitors, that collapses to product over sum. For n equal capacitors, it collapses further to simply C over n.
In series the charge is the common quantity: Q equals C one V one, equals C two V two, and so on. The total voltage is the sum of all the individual drops.
For capacitors in parallel, capacitances simply add. For n equal capacitors, that is just n times C.
In parallel the voltage is the common quantity, the total charge is the sum of the individual charges, and each capacitor's charge is simply its own C times that shared V.

Two reliable sanity checks, worth running every time: series must come out below the smallest member, and parallel must come out above the largest. If your answer violates either, you have mixed up the formulas.
One quick observation worth banking: for n equal capacitors, the ratio between the parallel value and the series value is exactly n squared.
Chalo combination formulas ek jagah collect karte hain।
Series mein capacitors ke liye, equivalent capacitance ka reciprocal individual reciprocals ka sum hota hai।
Sirf do capacitors ke liye, wo collapse hokar product over sum ban jaata hai। N equal capacitors ke liye, wo aur collapse hokar simply C over n ban jaata hai।
Series mein charge common quantity hai: Q equals C one V one, equals C two V two, aur aise hi। Total voltage saare individual drops ka sum hota hai।
Parallel mein capacitors ke liye, capacitances simply add hote hain। N equal capacitors ke liye, wo bas n times C hai।
Parallel mein voltage common quantity hai, total charge individual charges ka sum hai, aur har capacitor ka charge simply uska apna C times wo shared V hai।

Do reliable sanity checks, har baar chalane layak: series sabse chhote member se neeche aana chahiye, aur parallel sabse bade se upar। Agar tumhara answer kisi ko bhi violate kare, to tumne formulas mix up kar diye hain।
Ek quick observation bank karne layak: n equal capacitors ke liye, parallel value aur series value ke beech ka ratio exactly n squared hota hai।

sections.title: Formula toolkit: common potential and energy lost

board_events.text: Common potential and the energy lost on reconnection
That formula is nothing but charge conservation: total charge before equals total charge after, redistributed over the combined capacitance.
That expression is always positive or zero, because it contains a squared term — energy can only decrease, never increase.
It vanishes only when V one equals V two, which is exactly the case where no charge needs to flow at all.
Note carefully that this energy addition uses each capacitor's own voltage, not the total voltage across the network.

segments.text: Two more formulas cover what happens when charged capacitors are joined.
The common potential they settle at is the total charge divided by the total capacitance, which can also be written as C one V one plus C two V two, over C one plus C two.
That formula is nothing more than charge conservation written out. Total charge before equals total charge after, redistributed across the combined capacitance.
The energy lost in that redistribution is one half, times C one C two over C one plus C two, times the square of the voltage difference.
Look closely at that expression: it contains a squared term, so it is always positive or zero. Energy can only ever decrease in this process, never increase.
And it vanishes only when V one equals V two, which is precisely the case where no charge needs to flow in the first place.
For the stored energy of a combination, you can add each capacitor's own energy with its own voltage, or compute it directly from the equivalent capacitor. Both routes agree.
Note carefully that this energy addition uses each capacitor's own individual voltage, not the total voltage across the whole network. Mixing those up is a common source of wrong answers.
Do aur formulas cover karte hain ki kya hota hai jab charged capacitors jode jaate hain।
Wo common potential jispar wo settle hote hain, total charge divided by total capacitance hai, jise C one V one plus C two V two, over C one plus C two bhi likha ja sakta hai।
Wo formula charge conservation ko likhne se zyada kuch nahi hai। Pehle ka total charge baad ke total charge ke barabar hai, combined capacitance ke across redistribute kiya gaya।
Us redistribution mein lost energy hoti hai one half, times C one C two over C one plus C two, times voltage difference ka square.
Us expression ko dhyaan se dekho: usme ek squared term hai, isliye wo hamesha positive ya zero hota hai। Is process mein energy sirf ghat sakti hai, kabhi badh nahi sakti।
Aur wo sirf tab vanish hota hai jab V one equals V two, jo exactly wahi case hai jahan pehli jagah koi charge flow karne ki zaroorat hi nahi hai।

Kisi combination ki stored energy ke liye, tum har capacitor ki apni energy uske apne voltage ke saath add kar sakte ho, ya equivalent capacitor se directly compute kar sakte ho। Dono routes agree karte hain।
Dhyaan se note karo ki ye energy addition har capacitor ka apna individual voltage use karta hai, poore network ke across ka total voltage nahi। Unhe mix up karna wrong answers ka common source hai।

sections.title: Deriving the series combination formula

board_events.text: Derivation: capacitors in series
Connect C one, C two, and C three end to end across a source of voltage V.
The battery deposits plus Q on the first plate and minus Q on the last; by induction every capacitor carries the same charge Q.
The Q factors out cleanly precisely because the charge really is identical on every capacitor in the chain.
Because we add reciprocals, C series is always smaller than the smallest capacitor in the chain.

segments.text: Let's derive the series formula properly, rather than just quoting it.
Connect three capacitors, C one, C two, and C three, end to end across a source of voltage V.
The battery deposits plus Q on the first plate and minus Q on the last one. By the induction argument we walked through earlier, every capacitor in the chain ends up carrying that same charge Q.
The total applied voltage is the sum of the individual drops across the three capacitors.
For each capacitor, its voltage is Q over its own C. Substituting all three and factoring out the common Q gives this expression.
Notice that Q factors out cleanly, and it can only do so precisely because the charge really is identical on every capacitor in the chain. That physical fact is doing the algebraic work here.
The equivalent capacitor must store the same charge Q at the same total voltage V, so V equals Q over C series. Comparing the two expressions gives the series formula.
And because we are adding reciprocals rather than the values themselves, C series always comes out smaller than the smallest capacitor in the chain.
Chalo series formula ko properly derive karte hain, na ki bas quote karte rahen।
Teen capacitors, C one, C two, aur C three ko end to end connect karo ek voltage V wale source ke across।
Battery pehli plate par plus Q aur aakhri par minus Q deposit karti hai। Us induction argument se jo humne pehle dekha, chain ka har capacitor wahi same charge Q carry karta hai।
Total applied voltage teen capacitors ke across individual drops ka sum hai।
Har capacitor ke liye, uska voltage Q over uska apna C hai। Teenon ko substitute karke aur common Q ko factor out karke ye expression milta hai।
Notice karo Q cleanly factor out hota hai, aur wo sirf isliye ho sakta hai kyunki chain ke har capacitor par charge really identical hai। Wahi physical fact yahan algebraic kaam kar raha hai।
Equivalent capacitor ko wahi charge Q usi total voltage V par store karna chahiye, isliye V equals Q over C series. Dono expressions compare karne se series formula milta hai।
Aur kyunki hum values ki jagah reciprocals add kar rahe hain, C series hamesha chain ke sabse chhote capacitor se bhi chhota nikalta hai।

sections.title: Deriving the parallel combination formula

board_events.text: Derivation: capacitors in parallel
Connect C one, C two, and C three side by side across the source, so each has the same voltage V across it.
Here it is V that factors out, rather than Q — the exact mirror of what happened in the series derivation.
Because capacitances add directly, the parallel value always exceeds the largest member.

segments.text: The parallel derivation runs along exactly the mirror-image path.
Connect C one, C two, and C three side by side across the source, so that each one has exactly the same voltage V across it.
Each capacitor draws its own charge, given by its own capacitance times that shared voltage.
The battery supplies the total, which is the sum of the three individual charges. Factoring out the common V gives the bracketed sum of capacitances, times V.
Notice that here it is V which factors out, rather than Q. That is the exact mirror of what happened in the series derivation, and it traces straight back to which quantity is shared.
The equivalent capacitor holds this total charge at the same voltage V, so Q equals C parallel times V. Comparing gives capacitances adding directly.
And because capacitances add directly here, the parallel value always exceeds the largest member of the group.
Parallel derivation exactly mirror-image path par chalti hai।
C one, C two, aur C three ko source ke across side by side connect karo, taaki har ek ke across exactly wahi voltage V ho।
Har capacitor apna khud ka charge draw karta hai, jo uska apna capacitance times wo shared voltage se milta hai।
Battery total supply karti hai, jo teenon individual charges ka sum hai। Common V ko factor out karke capacitances ka bracketed sum, times V milta hai।
Notice karo yahan V factor out hota hai, Q nahi। Ye exactly wo mirror hai jo series derivation mein hua tha, aur ye seedha wapas jaata hai ki kaunsi quantity share ho rahi hai।
Equivalent capacitor is total charge ko usi voltage V par hold karta hai, isliye Q equals C parallel times V. Compare karne se capacitances directly add hote hue milte hain।
Aur kyunki yahan capacitances directly add hote hain, parallel value hamesha group ke sabse bade member se zyada hoti hai।

sections.title: Deriving the common potential and the energy loss

board_events.text: Derivation: common potential and energy loss
Two capacitors, with charges Q one equal to C one V one and Q two equal to C two V two, are joined like plate to like plate.
The squared voltage difference guarantees the result is never negative, so energy never spontaneously increases.
The loss is unavoidable, dissipated as heat and radiation, and vanishes only if the two voltages were already equal.

segments.text: Now let's derive where that energy loss formula actually comes from.
Take two capacitors, holding charges Q one equal to C one V one, and Q two equal to C two V two, and join them like plate to like plate.
Charge is conserved and they end at one common voltage. Total charge divided by total capacitance gives that common potential directly.
The energy before joining is simply each capacitor's own stored energy, added together.
The energy after joining is that of a single equivalent capacitor, C one plus C two, sitting at the common voltage.
Subtracting the second from the first, substituting the common potential and simplifying, everything collapses to this compact expression.
That squared voltage difference guarantees the result is never negative, which is exactly what physics demands: energy never spontaneously increases in this process.
The loss is genuinely unavoidable, dissipated as heat and a little radiation, and it vanishes only in the trivial case where the two voltages were already equal to begin with.
Ab derive karte hain ki wo energy loss formula actually kahan se aata hai।
Do capacitors lo, jinme charges Q one equal to C one V one, aur Q two equal to C two V two hain, aur unhe like plate to like plate jod do।
Charge conserved rehta hai aur wo ek common voltage par khatam hote hain। Total charge divided by total capacitance seedha wo common potential deta hai।
Jodne se pehle energy simply har capacitor ki apni stored energy hai, saath jodi hui।
Jodne ke baad energy ek single equivalent capacitor ki hai, C one plus C two, jo common voltage par baitha hai।
Doosre ko pehle se subtract karke, common potential substitute karke aur simplify karke, sab kuch is compact expression mein collapse ho jaata hai।
Wo squared voltage difference guarantee karta hai ki result kabhi negative nahi hoga, jo exactly wahi hai jo physics demand karti hai: is process mein energy kabhi spontaneously nahi badhti।
Wo loss genuinely unavoidable hai, heat aur thodi radiation ke roop mein dissipate hota hai, aur wo sirf us trivial case mein vanish hota hai jahan dono voltages shuru se hi equal the।

sections.title: CBSE level: three capacitors in series and in parallel

board_events.text: CBSE level: three capacitors, both arrangements
Three capacitors of two microfarads, three microfarads, and six microfarads are available.
Watch that last step carefully: the reciprocal came to one, so the capacitance itself is one, not six.
Both sanity checks hold: one microfarad is below the smallest, and eleven microfarads is above the largest.

segments.text: A clean numerical to anchor both combination formulas at once.
Three capacitors are available: two microfarads, three microfarads, and six microfarads. We want the equivalent capacitance both in series and in parallel.
For series, add the reciprocals over a common denominator of six: three sixths plus two sixths plus one sixth, which comes to exactly one.
Since the reciprocal equals one, the series capacitance is one microfarad.
Watch that last step carefully. The reciprocal came out to one, so the capacitance itself is one microfarad. Forgetting to flip back is a very common slip.
For parallel, capacitances simply add: two plus three plus six gives eleven microfarads.
Now run the sanity checks. One microfarad sits below the smallest member, which was two. Eleven microfarads sits above the largest, which was six. Both checks hold, so the answers are trustworthy.
Ek clean numerical jo dono combination formulas ko ek saath anchor karta hai।
Teen capacitors available hain: two microfarads, three microfarads, aur six microfarads. Humein series aur parallel dono mein equivalent capacitance chahiye।
Series ke liye, reciprocals ko six ke common denominator par add karo: three sixths plus two sixths plus one sixth, jo exactly one aata hai।
Kyunki reciprocal one ke barabar hai, series capacitance one microfarad hai।
Us last step ko dhyaan se dekho। Reciprocal one nikla, isliye capacitance khud one microfarad hai। Wapas flip karna bhoolna ek bahut common slip hai।
Parallel ke liye, capacitances simply add hote hain: two plus three plus six deta hai eleven microfarads.

Ab sanity checks chalao। One microfarad sabse chhote member se neeche baithta hai, jo two tha। Eleven microfarads sabse bade se upar baithta hai, jo six tha। Dono checks hold karte hain, isliye answers trustworthy hain।

sections.title: NEET speed trap: four identical capacitors

board_events.text: NEET speed trap: n equal capacitors
Four identical capacitors, each of four microfarads, are connected first all in series, then all in parallel.
The trap is adding series values directly, getting sixteen microfarads for the series case.
The two answers differ by a factor of sixteen, which is n squared, exactly as the general rule predicts.
Speed rule: n equal capacitors give C over n in series and n C in parallel — no working needed.

segments.text: This one tests whether you reach for the shortcut or grind through arithmetic you do not need.
Four identical capacitors, each of four microfarads, are connected first all in series, and then all in parallel. Find both equivalent capacitances.
The trap here is adding the series values directly and getting sixteen microfarads for the series case. That is the parallel answer wearing the wrong label.
For n equal capacitors there is no arithmetic to do at all. Series is simply C over n, which is four over four, or one microfarad.
Parallel is simply n times C, which is four times four, or sixteen microfarads.
Notice the two answers differ by a factor of sixteen, which is n squared. That is exactly what the general rule predicts, and it doubles as a check on your work.
Speed rule for exam day: n equal capacitors give C over n in series and n C in parallel. No working needed at all, which is exactly the time saving N E E T is testing for.
Ye test karta hai ki tum shortcut lete ho ya aisi arithmetic mein pisste ho jiski zaroorat hi nahi।
Chaar identical capacitors, har ek four microfarads ka, pehle sab series mein connect kiye jaate hain, phir sab parallel mein। Dono equivalent capacitances find karo।
Yahan trap hai series values ko directly add karke series case ke liye sixteen microfarads paana। Wo parallel ka answer hai galat label pehne hue।
N equal capacitors ke liye koi arithmetic karni hi nahi hai। Series simply C over n hai, jo four over four, ya one microfarad hai।
Parallel simply n times C hai, jo four times four, ya sixteen microfarads hai।
Notice karo dono answers sixteen ke factor se differ karte hain, jo n squared hai। Ye exactly wahi hai jo general rule predict karta hai, aur ye tumhare kaam ka check bhi hai।

Exam day ke liye speed rule: n equal capacitors series mein C over n aur parallel mein n C dete hain। Koi working ki bilkul zaroorat nahi, jo exactly wo time saving hai jiske liye N E E T test kar raha hai।

board_events.caption: C one and C two in series, that pair in parallel with C three, across twelve volts

board_events.text: Check: eight volts plus four volts equals twelve volts, matching the battery exactly.

segments.text: J E E Main almost guarantees a network-reduction problem like this one.

Capacitors C one equal to three microfarads and C two equal to six microfarads sit in series, and that series pair sits in parallel with C three equal to four microfarads, all across a twelve volt battery.
Start by reducing the series pair, using product over sum: three times six over three plus six, which gives two microfarads.
That reduced two microfarads now sits in parallel with four microfarads, and parallel values simply add, giving an equivalent capacitance of six microfarads.
For part b, C three sits directly across the battery in its own parallel branch, so it has the full twelve volts, giving forty eight microcoulombs.
For part c, the series branch also has twelve volts across it, storing twenty four microcoulombs. That same charge sits on both C one and C two, so their voltages are eight volts and four volts.
Always run this check: eight volts plus four volts equals twelve volts, matching the battery exactly. If the individual drops do not sum to the applied voltage, something has gone wrong upstream.
J E E Main almost guarantee karta hai ek network-reduction problem is jaisa।

Capacitors C one equal to three microfarads aur C two equal to six microfarads series mein baithe hain, aur wo series pair C three equal to four microfarads ke saath parallel mein hai, sab ek twelve volt battery ke across।
Series pair ko reduce karke shuru karo, product over sum use karte hue: three times six over three plus six, jo deta hai two microfarads.
Wo reduced two microfarads ab four microfarads ke saath parallel mein hai, aur parallel values simply add hote hain, jo six microfarads ka equivalent capacitance deta hai।
Part b ke liye, C three apni parallel branch mein seedha battery ke across baitha hai, isliye uske paas poore twelve volts hain, jo deta hai forty eight microcoulombs.

Part c ke liye, series branch ke across bhi twelve volts hain, jo twenty four microcoulombs store karta hai। Wahi same charge C one aur C two dono par baithta hai, isliye unke voltages eight volts aur four volts hain।

Ye check hamesha chalao: eight volts plus four volts equals twelve volts, jo battery se exactly match karta hai। Agar individual drops applied voltage tak sum na hon, to upstream kuch galat ho gaya hai।

sections.title: JEE Advanced: common potential and energy lost

board_events.text: JEE Advanced: reconnection, common potential, energy lost
A four microfarad capacitor charged to one hundred volts is connected, positive plate to positive plate, across a six microfarad capacitor charged to fifty volts.
Seventy volts sits between the original fifty and one hundred, which is exactly where a weighted average should land.
Check: those total seven hundred microcoulombs, matching the four hundred plus three hundred we started with.
Three millijoules went to heat: charge is conserved, energy is not.

segments.text: This one closes the subtopic by putting reconnection through real numbers.
A four microfarad capacitor charged to one hundred volts is connected, positive plate to positive plate, across a six microfarad capacitor charged to fifty volts.
For part a, conserve charge. Four hundred microcoulombs plus three hundred microcoulombs, divided by ten microfarads total, gives a common potential of seventy volts.
Notice seventy volts sits between the original fifty and one hundred. That is exactly where a weighted average should land, and it is a quick sanity check on the arithmetic.
For part b, each final charge is its own capacitance times the common voltage: two hundred eighty microcoulombs and four hundred twenty microcoulombs.
Check the conservation: those total seven hundred microcoulombs, matching exactly the four hundred plus three hundred we started with. Charge is fully accounted for.
For part c, substitute into the energy loss formula with a voltage difference of fifty volts, giving three millijoules lost.
Three millijoules went to heat in the connecting wires. This is the lesson in one line: charge is conserved, energy is not.
Ye example reconnection ko real numbers se guzaar kar subtopic close karta hai।
Ek four microfarad capacitor jo one hundred volts tak charged hai, positive plate to positive plate connect kiya jaata hai ek six microfarad capacitor ke across jo fifty volts tak charged hai।
Part a ke liye, charge conserve karo। Four hundred microcoulombs plus three hundred microcoulombs, divided by ten microfarads total, jo deta hai common potential of seventy volts.
Notice karo seventy volts original fifty aur one hundred ke beech baithta hai। Ye exactly wahan hai jahan ek weighted average ko land karna chahiye, aur ye arithmetic ka quick sanity check hai।
Part b ke liye, har final charge uska apna capacitance times common voltage hai: two hundred eighty microcoulombs aur four hundred twenty microcoulombs.
Conservation check karo: unka total seven hundred microcoulombs hai, jo exactly un four hundred plus three hundred se match karta hai jinse humne shuru kiya tha। Charge poori tarah account ho gaya।
Part c ke liye, energy loss formula mein substitute karo fifty volts ke voltage difference ke saath, jo deta hai three millijoules lost.
Three millijoules connecting wires mein heat ban gaye। Yahi lesson hai ek line mein: charge conserved hai, energy nahi।

sections.title: Pitfalls: swapped formulas and the conservation trap

board_events.text: Common pitfalls in combining capacitors
Swapping the series and parallel formulas. Capacitors add in parallel and add reciprocally in series — the opposite of resistors.
Anchor it with the shared quantity: series shares charge, parallel shares voltage.
Forgetting same charge in series and same voltage in parallel is what breaks per-capacitor calculations.
Skipping the sanity check. Series must come out below the smallest; parallel above the largest.
Assuming energy is conserved on reconnection. Only charge is conserved — there is always a loss unless the two voltages were already equal.
Pro-tip: reduce networks in stages, redrawing after each step, and label the charge and voltage you know at every node.

segments.text: Let's consolidate the traps this subtopic sets.
First, and by far the most common: swapping the series and parallel formulas. Capacitors add in parallel and add reciprocally in series, which is the exact opposite of resistors.
Do not memorise the formulas in isolation. Anchor them with the shared quantity: series shares charge, parallel shares voltage. Everything else follows from that one anchor.

Second: forgetting same charge in series and same voltage in parallel. That is exactly what lets you find the voltage or charge on an individual capacitor inside a network. Get it backwards and every per-capacitor value is wrong.
Third: skipping the sanity check. Series must come out below the smallest, and parallel above the largest. A single glance catches most slips before they cost you marks.
Fourth: assuming energy is conserved on reconnection. It is not. Only charge is conserved, and there is always a loss unless the two voltages happened to be equal already.

<whisper> Pro-tip: reduce networks in stages, redrawing the circuit after each step, and label the charge and voltage you know at every node. For two capacitors, memorise product over sum — far faster than reciprocals under time pressure.
Chalo is subtopic ke traps ko consolidate karte hain।
Pehla, aur sabse zyada common: series aur parallel formulas ko swap kar dena। Capacitors parallel mein add hote hain aur series mein reciprocally add hote hain, jo resistors ka exact opposite hai।
Formulas ko isolation mein mat yaad karo। Unhe shared quantity se anchor karo: series charge share karta hai, parallel voltage share karta hai। Baaki sab us ek anchor se follow karta hai।

Doosra: series mein same charge aur parallel mein same voltage bhoolna। Yahi wo cheez hai jo tumhe network ke andar individual capacitor ka voltage ya charge find karne deti hai। Isse ulta karo aur har per-capacitor value galat ho jaati hai।
Teesra: sanity check skip karna। Series sabse chhote se neeche aana chahiye, aur parallel sabse bade se upar। Ek nazar zyadatar slips pakad leti hai marks costs karne se pehle।
Chautha: ye assume karna ki reconnection par energy conserved hai। Wo nahi hai। Sirf charge conserved hai, aur hamesha ek loss hota hai jab tak dono voltages already equal na hon।

<whisper> Pro-tip: networks ko stages mein reduce karo, har step ke baad circuit dobara draw karte hue, aur har node par jo charge aur voltage tum jaante ho unhe label karo। Do capacitors ke liye, product over sum yaad karo — time pressure mein reciprocals se kaafi faster hai।

segments.text: Here is your complete toolkit for the chapter, all five subtopics on one board. This section restates rather than re-teaches, so use it as your final sweep before an exam.
Subtopic one, potential. Point charge, system of charges, and short dipole. Work equals charge times potential difference, and the field is minus the potential gradient.
Subtopic two, potential energy. Two charges, a system of charges, a charge in an external field, and a dipole in a uniform field, plus the full energy bookkeeping.
Subtopic three, capacitance. The definition, the parallel plate in air and with a dielectric, and the field in the gap.
Still subtopic three, the stored energy in its three equivalent forms, and the energy density of the field itself.
Subtopic four, conductors. Field zero inside, sigma over epsilon zero just outside, the whole body one equipotential, plus the two spherical capacitance results.
Subtopic five, combinations. Series adds reciprocals, with product over sum for two and C over n for n equal ones; parallel simply adds.
Still subtopic five, the common potential on reconnection and the energy inevitably lost in getting there.
And the two constants that appear throughout every calculation in this chapter.

Finally, the two dimensional formulas most likely to be asked: potential is M L squared T to the minus three, A to the minus one, and capacitance is M to the minus one, L to the minus two, T to the fourth, A squared.

Subtopic one, potential। Point charge, charges ka system, aur short dipole। Work equals charge times potential difference, aur field minus potential gradient hai।
Subtopic two, potential energy। Do charges, charges ka system, external field mein ek charge, aur uniform field mein dipole, plus poori energy bookkeeping।
Subtopic three, capacitance। Definition, air mein aur dielectric ke saath parallel plate, aur gap mein field।
Abhi bhi subtopic three, stored energy apne teen equivalent forms mein, aur khud field ki energy density।
Subtopic four, conductors। Andar field zero, bas bahar sigma over epsilon zero, poora body ek equipotential, plus do spherical capacitance results।
Subtopic five, combinations। Series reciprocals add karta hai, do ke liye product over sum aur n equal ke liye C over n ke saath; parallel simply add karta hai।
Abhi bhi subtopic five, reconnection par common potential aur wahan tak pahunchne mein inevitably lost energy।
Aur wo do constants jo is chapter ki har calculation mein appear karte hain।

Finally, wo do dimensional formulas jo sabse zyada pooche jaane ki sambhavna hai: potential hai M L squared T to the minus three, A to the minus one, aur capacitance hai M to the minus one, L to the minus two, T to the fourth, A squared।

sections.title: Quick recall: the whole chapter on one board

board_events.text: Quick recall: the whole chapter in one sweep
Potential is a scalar — just add contributions with their signs. No angles, no components, no vector diagrams.
V and E are different questions — answer each on its own. V zero does not mean E zero, and E zero does not mean V zero.
On an equipotential surface you ride free: field is perpendicular everywhere, zero work to move along it, and surfaces never intersect.
Potential energy goes as one over r, while force and field go as one over r squared. Like charges give U positive; unlike charges give U negative.
Capacitance is geometry, not charge. Disconnected? Q is king. Connected? V is king.
Energy goes as V squared, and charging through a battery always wastes exactly half as heat. A dielectric only ever boosts C, by the factor K.
Inside a conductor nothing happens: field zero, charge on the skin, one equipotential blob. Just outside, the field is sigma over epsilon zero — double the lone sheet.
A cage shields in, not out. Charge q in a cavity gives inner surface minus q, outer surface plus q for a neutral shell.
Series shares charge and lands below the smallest; parallel shares voltage and lands above the largest. Reconnect and charge is conserved, energy is not.

segments.text: <excited> This is your last-minute revision board. One line per idea, the whole chapter in one sweep.
Potential is a scalar. Just add contributions with their signs. No angles, no components, no vector diagrams anywhere.

V and E are different questions, and you must answer each on its own. V equal to zero does not mean E is zero, and E equal to zero does not mean V is zero. This is the single most exam-tested confusion in the chapter.
On an equipotential surface, you ride free. The field is perpendicular everywhere, it costs zero work to move along it, and two equipotential surfaces can never intersect.

Potential energy goes as one over r, while force and field go as one over r squared. Like charges give U positive; unlike charges give U negative, meaning a bound system. And a dipole always rests aligned with the field.
Capacitance is geometry, never charge or voltage. And the fork that decides every dielectric problem: disconnected means Q is king, connected means V is king. Decide it before touching a formula.

Energy goes as V squared, and charging through a battery always wastes exactly half the supplied energy as heat, whatever the resistance. And a dielectric only ever boosts capacitance, by the factor K.
Inside a conductor, nothing happens. Field zero, all charge on the skin, the whole body one equipotential blob. Just outside, the field is sigma over epsilon zero, double the lone sheet value.
A cage shields in, not out. A charge q sitting in a cavity gives inner surface minus q and outer surface plus q for a neutral shell, and from outside the field looks exactly like q at the centre.

And finally, combinations. Series shares charge and lands below the smallest member; parallel shares voltage and lands above the largest. Capacitors are upside-down resistors. Reconnect two charged capacitors and charge is conserved, but energy is not. <whisper> Carry those four lines into the exam and most of this chapter is already answered.
<excited> Ye tumhara last-minute revision board hai। Har idea ke liye ek line, poora chapter ek sweep mein।
Potential ek scalar hai। Bas contributions ko unke signs ke saath add karo। Koi angles nahi, koi components nahi, kahin koi vector diagram nahi।

V aur E alag questions hain, aur tumhe har ek ko apne aap answer karna hoga। V equal to zero ka matlab E zero nahi, aur E equal to zero ka matlab V zero nahi। Ye chapter ki sabse zyada exam-tested confusion hai।
Equipotential surface par, tum free ride karte ho। Field har jagah perpendicular hai, uske along move karne mein zero work lagta hai, aur do equipotential surfaces kabhi intersect nahi kar sakti।

Potential energy one over r ki tarah jaati hai, jabki force aur field one over r squared ki tarah। Like charges U positive dete hain; unlike charges U negative dete hain, matlab ek bound system। Aur dipole hamesha field ke saath aligned rest karta hai।

Capacitance geometry hai, kabhi charge ya voltage nahi। Aur wo fork jo har dielectric problem decide karta hai: disconnected matlab Q is king, connected matlab V is king. Formula touch karne se pehle isse decide karo।

Energy V squared ki tarah jaati hai, aur battery se charging hamesha supplied energy ka exactly half heat ke roop mein waste karti hai, resistance chahe kuch bhi ho। Aur dielectric sirf capacitance boost karta hai, factor K se।
Conductor ke andar, kuch nahi hota। Field zero, saara charge skin par, poora body ek equipotential blob। Bas bahar, field sigma over epsilon zero hai, lone sheet value se double।

Cage andar shield karta hai, bahar nahi। Cavity mein baitha charge q neutral shell ke liye inner surface par minus q aur outer surface par plus q deta hai, aur bahar se field exactly aisa dikhta hai jaise q centre par ho।

Aur finally, combinations। Series charge share karta hai aur sabse chhote se neeche land karta hai; parallel voltage share karta hai aur sabse bade se upar। Capacitors ulte resistors hain। Do charged capacitors reconnect karo aur charge conserved hai, lekin energy nahi। <whisper> In chaar lines ko exam mein le jao aur is chapter ka zyadatar hissa already answered hai।
